finding.claim: GET /users has no authentication or tenant authorization check, so any unauthenticated caller can list id and name of all users in any org by supplying the org query parameter.
finding.source: req.query.org (db.js:9), reachable via GET /users?org=<id> on port 3002 (db.js:23) with no credentials
finding.sink: req.pg.query SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE org = $1 (db.js:9), response returned as JSON (db.js:10)

trace.note: Route registered on app with no auth middleware; no app.use guard exists in this file
req.query.org used as the org filter without comparing it to the caller's identity or org
All matching id and name rows returned to the caller

finding.guards_checked: No auth/session middleware registered on app in this file; no owner or tenant comparison on the org value; SQL is parameterized so no SQL injection; req.pg is not defined in this file, so an upstream authenticating middleware cannot be ruled out from this code alone, but none exists in the audited tree.

verdict.guard_found: none. db.js:8 registers GET /users with no auth middleware, db.js:9 passes req.query.org straight into the WHERE clause with no comparison to any caller identity, and db.js:10 returns all rows. db.js:23 listens on 3002. The only file in the tree is db.js, so no upstream auth middleware exists. The parameterized query at db.js:9 blocks SQL injection but not this authorization gap.
verdict.reason: An anonymous caller can request GET /users?org=<any id> at db.js:8-10 and receive every matching id and name, with no auth or tenant check between db.js:9 and the response, and db.js:23 exposes the port. The one caveat is that req.pg is not defined in this file, but no middleware that sets it exists in the audited tree.
